ch18.note: The Naigai Cotton Mill (Naigai Wata Kaisha) was a Japanese-owned cotton-spinning combine, one of the largest foreign employers of Chinese mill labor in Shanghai and a recurring flashpoint of the labor unrest of the 1920s. It was at its No. 7 mill that the killing of the worker Gu Zhenghong in May 1925 helped touch off the May Thirtieth Movement (see the note further on). Corroborated.

ch18.anchor: the Japanese had killed Gu Zhenghong
ch18.note: Gu Zhenghong (1905–1925), a Communist and a worker at the No. 7 mill of the Japanese-owned Naigai company in Shanghai, was shot by the mill’s Japanese management on 15 May 1925 while leading workers who demanded to be let back to work. His death and the mass funeral protests were the immediate spark of the May Thirtieth Movement (for the movement itself, see the note at its first mention in chapter 1). Corroborated.

Deng Zhongxia (1894–1933), a Peking University graduate and one of the founders of the Communist labor movement, led the great Canton–Hong Kong strike of 1925–26 (noted at chapter 10). Hunted for years by the Kuomintang, he was arrested in Shanghai and shot in Nanjing on 21 September 1933. Corroborated.

ch18.anchor: the Central Committee had already settled at Wayaobao
ch18.note: Wayaobao (瓦窑堡), a town in Zichang county in northern Shaanxi, was the seat of the Party Central after the Long March, from late 1935 to the middle of 1936. There, on 17 December 1935, the Wayaobao Conference set the policy of a national united front against Japan. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: the Comintern's Far Eastern Bureau all changed house
ch19.note: The Comintern’s Far Eastern Bureau was its regional headquarters in Shanghai, overseeing the Communist parties of East and Southeast Asia—supervising them, channeling funds, and running a clandestine courier network back to Moscow. Its Shanghai apparatus was crippled by the 1931 arrests bound up with the Noulens couple (see the note in chapter 21). Corroborated.

ch20.note: Qiu Jin (1875–1907), a revolutionary, feminist, and poet who studied in Japan and joined the anti-Qing underground, was captured and beheaded by Qing authorities in 1907 after a failed uprising. She became one of the most revered martyrs of the movement that overthrew the dynasty. Corroborated.

The Young China Association (少年中国学会), founded in 1919, was among the largest and most influential of the May Fourth–era study societies. Its members ranged across the political spectrum and later divided sharply between Communism and its opponents—the split that surfaced at the 1921 meeting described here. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: the 19th Route Army rose to fight back
ch21.note: The 19th Route Army won national fame for its month-long defense of Shanghai against the Japanese in the January 28 Incident of 1932 (see the note in chapter 20). Its commanders later broke with Chiang Kai-shek and, in November 1933, set up the short-lived anti-Chiang Fujian People’s Government, which was crushed early in 1934. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: would be reorganized as the Eighth Route Army
ch21.note: The Eighth Route Army was the main Communist force in north China during the war with Japan. Under the Kuomintang–Communist united front of 1937 the Red Army was nominally folded into the Nationalist forces as the Eighth Route Army—its companion in the south being the New Fourth Army (noted at chapter 4)—while remaining under Communist command. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: president of the Executive Yuan of the Nanjing Kuomintang government
ch21.note: The Executive Yuan was the cabinet, the highest administrative organ of the Nationalist government under the five-“yuan” structure adopted in 1928; its president served as head of government. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: its American members Agnes Smedley and Harold Isaacs
ch22.note: Agnes Smedley (1892–1950), an American journalist and writer, was a fierce partisan of the Chinese revolution who reported from the Communist areas and moved in Comintern intelligence circles in Shanghai. Her sympathies later drew United States government suspicion; she died in England in 1950. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: when Academia Sinica was founded in Shanghai
ch22.note: Academia Sinica, founded in 1928 with Cai Yuanpei as its first president, was the Republic of China’s national academy—its most prestigious body for scientific and scholarly research. It later removed to Taiwan. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: the central leaders Mao Zedong, Zhang Wentian, Zhou Enlai
ch22.note: Zhang Wentian (1900–1976), also known as Luo Fu, was a Moscow-trained theorist who, after the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, became the responsible head of the Party Central—in effect its top leader through 1943—working in close partnership with Mao Zedong. He was later a diplomat and vice-minister of foreign affairs, and was purged alongside Peng Dehuai at the Lushan Conference of 1959. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: following Yang Shangkun, director of the Political Department
ch22.note: Yang Shangkun (1907–1998), one of the Soviet-trained returned students known as the “28 Bolsheviks” and among the few to side early with Mao Zedong, was a Red Army political commissar who rose after 1949 to head the Party Central’s General Office and, under Deng Xiaoping, the Central Military Commission. He served as president of the People’s Republic from 1988 to 1993. Corroborated.
